newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FORECAST-Bank of Israel seen cutting rates.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Bank of Israel seen cutting rates.

text.p: Israeli interest rates could fall as much as 0.5 percentage point for June, analysts said on Sunday, but they warned that a cautious central bank might still hold the line another month or two.
Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel is due to announce the June monetary programme on Monday. He last cut the base rate at the end of February to 13.9 percent.
"All the parameters say he must cut," said Adam Reuter, managing director of Financial Immunities, a financial consulting firm.
He said he expected the base rate would be lowered 0.2-0.3 point but warned there might be no cut at all "because he's Frenkel."

The central bank governor has a reputation as a monetary hawk, prompting attacks from the Treasury and business leaders who say he has ignored a slowing economy and the upward pressure interest rates have exerted on the Israeli currency.
But analysts said they expected Frenkel would begin moderating his stance in the face of the slowdown, which began in the second half of last year.

"The big picture is that the trend is toward lower interest rates over the next few months," said Hezi Gutman, chief economist at First International Bank of Israel. "Whether it will begin this month I can't say for certain."
Gutman said if the central bank does announce a cut on Monday it will be between 0.3 and 0.5 point.
Frenkel may still be reluctant to cut rates quickly because the data on slowing economic growth is still cloudy, he said.

The Central Bureau of Statistics last week reported gross domestic product grew at a 2.8 percent annualised rate in the first quarter. That was lower than the 4.4 percent increase for full-year 1996 but up from a 1.8 percent rate in the previous quarter.
"The data for January-March show there is still no recession," Gutman said. "We're less certain now than we were before last week that the economy is continuing to slow."
Gutman said Frenkel would also pay close attention to jobless figures. "Unemployment may have a bigger impact on inflation than the budget," he said.
The latest figure, from fourth-quarter 1996, puts unemployment at seven percent. But Gutman said unpublished estimates by the Central Bureau of Statistics show the rate had risen since then.

Roy Meir, of Simodan brokerage house, contended Frenkel was watching figures on inflation more carefully than those on growth. He nevertheless agreed with other analysts that the Bank of Israel would cut rates by about 0.3 point.
"Inflation will be lower over the next few months compared with the previous months," he said, adding that the decline would be due to seasonal drops in fresh produce prices.
Meir said the Bank of Israel would continue to cut rates until the base rate fell to 13 percent.
